items.claim: The paper investigates how the regional political climate moderates the relationship between an individual's self-reported political conservatism and their hesitancy toward and uptake of COVID-19 vaccines and boosters.
The interaction between conservatism and climate is significant for hesitancy and booster status, indicating that the effect of conservatism on these outcomes is stronger in conservative regions.

Liberals show low vaccine hesitancy and high booster uptake regardless of the political climate of their region, whereas conservatives' behavior is heavily influenced by their local political environment.

Conservatives in liberal regions are significantly more likely to receive boosters than conservatives in conservative regions, suggesting environmental factors influence booster uptake among conservatives.
Unlike hesitancy and booster status, the interaction between political conservatism and regional climate was not significant for initial vaccine status.

Conservative regions in both the US and Canada exhibited significantly higher levels of partisan polarization regarding COVID-19 health measures, with a strong negative correlation between polarization and vaccination rates in the US, a pattern not observed in Canada.

The authors analyzed over 50 million tweets from late 2020 to early 2021, geolocating users and classifying them by party affiliation to measure polarization using a semantic embedding-based index (C-index) across topics of lockdowns, masks, and vaccines.

Conservative regions in both the US and Canada exhibited significantly higher levels of partisan polarization regarding COVID-19 health measures, with a strong negative correlation between polarization and vaccination rates in the US, a pattern not observed in Canada.
The authors state that their correlations do not imply causation and that the temporal mismatch between Twitter data (2020) and vaccination rates (2021) limits causal claims.

The paper investigates whether Democratic Party campaign advertisements labeling Donald Trump as a 'convicted criminal' cause stigmatizing spillover effects on Democrats' perceptions of individuals with criminal records, and whether a counter-narrative featuring a formerly system-involved representative can mitigate these effects.

Exposure to Democratic Party advertisements labeling Trump as a 'convicted criminal' negatively impacts Democrats' perceptions of individuals with criminal records, but this negative effect is largely ameliorated when participants are first exposed to a counter-narrative featuring the perspective of a formerly system-involved state representative.
The negative effects of the Trump advertisement on perceptions of individuals with criminal records were more pronounced for participants who identified as system-impacted.

The study acknowledges limitations including the lack of a full factorial design (preventing isolation of the counter-narrative's effect alone), the inability to disentangle the impact of the image from the text in the advertisement, and the use of an online panel which raises concerns about AI-generated responses and social desirability bias.

The paper builds upon social categorization theory to explain how salient labels applied to a group exemplar (Trump) can spill over to affect perceptions of the broader group (individuals with criminal records), while also incorporating literature on perspective-getting as a mechanism to counteract this stigma.

The association between political engagement and online hostility is stronger among users with higher levels of leader-directed affective polarization, particularly for participatory indicators.
The authors extend the revisionist perspective on the costs of political engagement to online political hostility, building on classical theories that acknowledge engagement can become excessive.

The paper disputes the view that online hostility is primarily driven by socioeconomic marginalization, status threat, or personality-based traits like sadism, arguing instead that it is also associated with normative democratic engagement.

The findings are limited to three schools on one reservation and cannot be generalized to AI youth in racially heterogeneous schools or other reservation contexts.

The paper disputes the claim, common in research on non-AI adolescent populations, that substance use is consistently linked to friendship formation and popularity through selection and influence processes.
